rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor is. Its “The "70% lower than cards" claim — where account-to-account actually beats interchange” angle attacks the qualified savings claim and demands the fee, threshold, sample, and methodology; B’s “Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes. Now it wants to own the payment.” starts freelancing into a company-strategy story the brief did not supply. A still overclaims FedNow once, but B keeps turning plausible background into asserted fact, and that is how pitches get deleted.
gaps_in_A: “FedNow gets its first big merchant-payments use case” is not grounded. The update says Pay by Bank uses FedNow; it does not prove first, big, commercial scale, or even named merchant adoption.
“credible alternative to cards at the point of sale” adds checkout-context color the update does not actually give. Merchant acceptance is supplied; point-of-sale behavior is not.
“Next step: `meanest-editor`” is the wrong workflow label for an angle set. The substance is fine, but the next operational move is proof-gathering or journalist-fit, not a critique skill.
gaps_in_B: “competing simultaneously with Stripe and Adyen on one side” is invented. Stripe and Adyen are not in the update, and dragging them in makes the angle feel smarter than its evidence.
“Plaid spent a decade building the data pipes” is outside the supplied facts. It may be true background, but this exercise asked for grounded angles, not memory cosplay.
“FedNow just got its most significant commercial test” is a giant claim with no volume, named merchant, or independent adoption data. That headline is wearing a suit it has not earned.

“what percentage of Plaid-connected merchant volume could realistically migrate to A2A” quietly invents Plaid-connected merchant volume. The brief gives financial-institution coverage, not merchant volume.
